Validation of the 5 insights
#AccuracyImportanceReview1. AI code agent market $98–110B, 70%+ enterprise adoption by 2028Partly accurate, market number likely overstated/mis-scoped6/10The adoption direction is right: Gartner projected 75% of enterprise software engineers will use AI code assistants by 2028, up from under 10% in early 2023. But the $98–110B by 2028 figure does not match the stronger public market estimates I found: MarketsandMarkets projected AI Code Tools at $12.6B by 2028, while a newer MarketsandMarkets “AI Code Assistants” report projects $127.05B by 2032, not 2028. Treat the $98–110B number as likely broader-category or inflated unless you can identify its source. Gartner+2MarketsandMarkets+22. GitHub Copilot usage-based pricingConfirmed8/10GitHub announced that all Copilot plans transition to usage-based billing on June 1, 2026, consuming GitHub AI Credits. GitHub docs also note the earlier model was “premium request” based before June 1, 2026. Missing context: this matters less if your core stack is Claude Code + Ollama, but it matters if you rely on Copilot for IDE autocomplete or want GitHub Models/Copilot as a paid fallback. The GitHub Blog+13. Competition shifting from benchmarks to workflow integration/governance/multi-step agentsMostly accurate9/10This is the most strategically correct insight. GitLab’s June 2026 research says organizations are generating AI code faster than they can control it: 91% use two or more AI coding tools, 78% report faster code output, 43% cannot reliably distinguish AI-generated from human-written code, and 92% report some governance challenge. Missing context: “voice” is not essential for your setup; the important pieces are memory, permissions, audit logs, policy gates, replayable workflows, and verification. GitLab+14. OpenAI Codex 5x user growth H1 2026Confirmed, but wording should shift from completion to agents7/10The June 2026 Codex paper reports that active Codex users grew more than fivefold in H1 2026. It also says more than 10% of users manage three or more concurrent Codex agents weekly, and 26.6% use skills. Missing context: the lesson is not “add code completion”; it is “build agentic workflows: delegated tasks, concurrent agents, skills, verification, and task packaging.” You already have completion/local small-model coverage via Ollama. arXiv5. Deterministic Control Plane: permissions/audit/policy unmanagedConfirmed and highest priority10/10A June 2026 paper explicitly argues that LLM coding harnesses grant broad file/shell access while the configuration layer—rules files, agent definitions, IDE markdown—is largely unmanaged. This aligns with GitLab’s governance findings and with your own Hook/state-machine work. Missing context: the control plane should be deterministic and outside the model’s discretion: PreToolUse gates, PostToolUse logs, Stop gates, permissions, evidence artifacts, and replayable state. arXiv+1
Corrected takeaways

Do not chase “AI coding market size” as a product decision signal. Adoption is clearly accelerating, but market-size estimates vary wildly depending on whether they measure code tools, code assistants, agents, or broader AI developer infrastructure.

Copilot pricing confirms the cost-governance trend. Usage-based pricing means you need token/request accounting, even if Copilot is not your main tool.

The real battleground is governed workflows, not raw model benchmarks. Your stack should optimize for routing, memory, permissions, evidence, test automation, and auditability.

Codex growth validates multi-agent/task delegation patterns. But you should copy the workflow primitives—skills, concurrent tasks, task packaging—not necessarily adopt Codex directly.

Deterministic control plane is the top engineering priority. Your agent must not rely on “remembering rules”; it needs hard gates and evidence-based closure.

Top 2 actions for your Windows Claude Code + Ollama + local agent setup
1. Finish the deterministic control plane before adding more agents
Implement this as your default workflow:
PreToolUse: block dangerous shell/file operations require memory/wrongbook check before edits require guard before risky commandsPostToolUse: record every Edit/Write/Bash/PowerShell/WebSearch/tool call update current.json stateStop: block final answer if files changed without tests/evidence block learning task if GPT audit/archive missing block script creation without execution or waiver
For your hardware and no-Docker Windows setup, this should be lightweight PowerShell + JSON state files, not a containerized control plane. This directly addresses the governance gap identified in June 2026 research.
2. Build a local “agent workbench” instead of adding more cloud coding tools
Use your existing pieces this way:
Claude Code / DeepSeek V4 Pro: main planner and executorOllama qwen2.5-coder: JSON repair, routing, log summaries, small code transformsLocal FastAPI agent: stable API for memory/search/routing/health checksPlaywright MCP: browser automation and web verificationGPT-5.5 pipeline: high-risk audit onlyNo Docker: run as Windows services or scheduled PowerShell tasks
Add one missing layer: cost + evidence ledger. Track per task:
JSON{ "task_id": "...", "models_used": ["deepseek", "ollama", "gpt-5.5"], "tools_called": 18, "files_changed": 3, "tests_run": true, "evidence": ["git diff", "pytest output", "screenshot"], "external_api_calls": 2, "risk_level": "medium"}
This gives you the main advantage the market is moving toward: not “more AI,” but controlled, observable, repeatable AI coding work.
